title: Object-Oriented Programming: Objects and Classes
learningObjectives: Define the paradigm or design concept.
Explain how it organizes code, data, or responsibilities.
Trace an example and describe its behavior.
Identify one benefit and one limitation.
Apply the approach to a small programming scenario.

understand.concept: Object-oriented programming organizes software around objects that combine state (data) and behavior (operations). In class-based languages, a class defines structure and behavior for creating instances. Some languages use prototype-based or other object models, so class syntax is not universal.
understand.whyItMatters: OOP can group responsibilities, model entities, and support reuse. Poor class hierarchies or excessive coupling can make change difficult.
understand.analogy: A class resembles a specification for similar objects with their own data; actual object systems may include dynamic dispatch and complex runtime rules.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy simplifies programming design; real programs have additional constraints and implementation details.

explain.narrative: Focus on the design approach rather than memorizing labels. Trace the example, identify how data and operations are organized, and consider how the design might change if requirements grow. Paradigms can be combined; trade-offs depend on the language, task, team, and scale.

examples.code:

const c=new Counter(); c.inc(); console.log(c.value);
examples.explanation: Object combines state with a method.

examples.title: Separate instances
examples.explanation: Each instance has its own data.

examples.title: Method reads state
examples.explanation: A method uses the instance's state.

examples.title: Grouped responsibility
examples.explanation: Related data and operations are grouped.

commonMistakes: Treating one paradigm as universally superior.
Confusing syntax with an entire design approach.
Creating unnecessary abstractions for tiny tasks.
Allowing shared state without clear responsibility.
